topic.title: Passing Arguments by Values
topic.description: How arguments are passed to methods

sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Let’s break down how Java handles arguments when you pass them to methods. It’s simpler than you think!

• How Java passes values (not variables) to methods
• Why changing a parameter inside a method doesn’t affect the original value
• Common mistakes and how to avoid them

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine you’re photocopying a document. The original stays safe, but you can scribble all over the copy. That’s how Java passes arguments!

When you pass a variable to a method, Java creates a *copy* of its value. The method works with this copy, leaving the original untouched.

• **Primitive types** (like `int`, `double`) are passed *by value* – a full copy is made
• **Objects** are passed *by reference value* – the copy points to the same object (but the reference itself is copied!)
• Changing the copy inside the method won’t affect the original variable

sections.title: 📊 Visual Simulation
sections.content: Step-by-step visualization of how Passing Arguments by Values works:

steps.title: Before the Method Call
steps.description: You have a variable with a value. Java prepares to make a copy.

steps.title: During the Method Call
steps.description: Java copies the value and passes it to the method. The method gets its own version.

steps.title: After the Method Call
steps.description: The original variable remains unchanged. The copy disappears when the method ends.

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ Java *always* passes arguments by value – even for objects!
✓ Changing a parameter inside a method won’t affect the original variable
✓ For objects, the *reference* is copied, not the object itself
✓ Primitive types are copied entirely (like photocopying a number)
✓ Think of parameters as disposable copies – safe to modify!

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Remember that method parameters are *local* to the method
For objects, changes to the object’s *state* persist (but reassigning the parameter won’t)
donts: Don’t assume changes to parameters affect the original variable
Don’t create multiple `Scanner` objects for the same input stream (like in the textbook example!)
Don’t confuse *passing by value* with *passing by reference* – Java doesn’t do the latter!
sections.protip: If you want a method to modify a variable, *return* the new value instead of trying to change the parameter!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is Passing Arguments by Values used in real apps?

examples.how: When calculating interest, the original balance isn’t changed until the transaction is confirmed. The method works with a copy of the balance value.
Player health is passed to a damage-calculation method. The method reduces a *copy* of the health value, then returns the new value to update the original.
User input is passed to validation methods. The original input stays unchanged while the method checks the copy.

problem.description: Fix this code so it correctly doubles the value of `number` without changing the original variable directly. The method should return the new value.
hints: Remember: Java passes by value, so the method can’t change `number` directly
The method should return the doubled value
Assign the method’s return value to a variable in `main`
problem.explanation: The method `doubleValue` receives a *copy* of `number`. It doubles the copy and returns the result. The original `number` remains unchanged, but we capture the returned value in `doubled`.

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Java passes arguments *by value* – always a copy, never the original
📌 Changing a parameter inside a method won’t affect the original variable
📌 Practice writing methods that return modified values instead of trying to change parameters
📌 Ready for next topic: *Passing Objects to Methods* (where things get more interesting!)
